name: Swallow Falls
blurb: Muddy Creek Falls is the tallest free-falling waterfall in Maryland at 53 feet. The mile-long loop past it runs through old-growth hemlock and white pine, some of it over 300 years old and the last of its kind in the state. It's the most visited park in Garrett County, and the reason the reservation system exists.

reservation.window: Memorial Day weekend 2026 (23 May) – Labor Day 2026
reservation.days: Weekends and holidays only. Weekdays are entry on arrival.
reservation.bookAhead: Opens 7 days before the visit; changes or cancellations until 8am the day before
reservation.note: Slots are expected to sell out consistently through the summer, so a weekend visit needs planning. On weekdays you can still turn up and pay on arrival.

fee.note: Sat of Memorial Day weekend – Labor Day: $3 per person Maryland residents, $5 per person out-of-state; Tue after Labor Day – Fri before Memorial Day: $3 per vehicle Maryland residents, $5 per vehicle out-of-state. Day-use fees are paid when you book a weekend reservation, plus a non-refundable service charge of about $1.50 per person.

You cannot turn up without a reservation in summer. This is a three-hour drive from Baltimore or DC and the booking window only opens seven days out.

reports.what: The ranger station, restrooms and store are all at the main parking area, not off at the campground. The trailheads start a few steps from that same lot.

fieldNotes.author: Matt
fieldNotes.body: The ranger station, the restrooms and the store are all at the main parking area, not off at the campground the way Maryland's own listing implies. Trailheads start a few steps from the same lot, so you can park and be walking in under a minute.

verdict.text: The waterfall is genuinely worth the drive, and the hemlock stand behind it is the better half. Everything you need is at the main lot, so you can park and be walking in a minute. Just don't turn up on a Saturday without a booking, because that changed in May and most of the internet hasn't noticed.

photos.alt: A wide waterfall dropping over a layered rock ledge into a brown pool, framed by summer trees on both sides and a bare rock shelf at the top left.
photos.caption: Muddy Creek Falls from the overlook, in summer. The water is tea-coloured — that's tannin off the hemlocks, not silt.

photos.alt: A smaller falls seen from downstream across a broad shelf of flat wet rock, with rhododendron leaning in from both banks and a green canopy above.
photos.caption: Looking back upstream from the flat rock shelf below. Rhododendron on both banks, and the rock is slick where it looks dry.

fieldNotes.body: The swim area is roped inside stone breakwaters, so it stays calm even when the rest of the lake is busy with boats. Plenty of sand, and shade at the back of the beach if you get there early enough to claim it.

verdict.text: The swim area sits inside stone breakwaters, so it stays flat even when the rest of the lake is full of boats. Plenty of sand. The shade at the back of the beach goes early, though.

name: Herrington Manor
blurb: A 53-acre lake made by damming Herrington Creek, with twenty year-round cabins built by the Civilian Conservation Corps. No gas motors on the lake, which keeps it quiet. Cross-country ski rental in winter, one of very few places in Maryland where that's a real option.

blurb: Four acres around an 80-foot stone arch built in 1813 for the National Road. It was the largest single-span stone arch in America when it was finished, and it's a National Historic Landmark. A ten-minute stop rather than a day out, and worth it.

name: Rock Maze
blurb: A natural labyrinth of house-sized sandstone boulders, moss over every surface, with passages narrow enough to turn sideways for. It isn't a signed DNR trail and it isn't on the state forest's map. Locals know it, and that's mostly how you find it.

warnings: Snaggy Mountain Road is one of the forest's ORV trail areas. Expect motorised vehicles on the road you park on.
There is no sign, no marked trailhead and no facilities. The parking area is small.
The boulders are moss-covered and hold water. They are slick well after rain, and the passages between them are genuinely tight.

reports.what: The trailhead is a small parking area on Snaggy Mountain Road, near where it meets Cranesville Road. The walk in runs through open hardwood with heavy fern cover before it reaches the boulders.

photos.alt: Two children walking away from the camera down a narrow passage between two towering moss-covered sandstone walls, with daylight above.
photos.caption: The passage itself. The walls are what the name is about, and the figures are there for scale — several of the gaps are barely shoulder-width.

photos.alt: A narrow earth footpath running through open hardwood forest, banked on both sides by dense waist-high ferns, with sunlight coming through the canopy.
photos.caption: The approach: open hardwood and heavy fern cover before the ground turns to boulders.

photos.alt: A tree growing directly out of a large moss-covered sandstone boulder, its roots running down the rock face, with rhododendron around it.
photos.caption: Sandstone under moss, with trees rooted straight over the rock. This is the surface the whole maze is made of — and why it stays slick.

photos.alt: Several pink-capped Russula mushrooms growing on dark leaf litter on the forest floor.
photos.caption: Russula on the forest floor in early August. Look, photograph, do not eat.

fieldNotes.author: Matt
fieldNotes.body: The trailhead is a small pull-in on Snaggy Mountain Road near Cranesville Road. No sign, so you are looking for the parking area rather than the trail. The walk in is open hardwood with fern up to your knees, and then the ground turns to boulders fairly suddenly. Some of the passages are barely shoulder-width and everything is mossy, which means slick long after it has stopped raining. Not one to do in a hurry.

verdict.text: House-sized boulders with passages between them narrow enough to turn sideways for, and no sign anywhere telling you it exists. The moss holds water for days, so it's slick long after the rain stops. Not one to rush, and not one to do in trainers.
